case_info.scenario: A 74-year-old man was referred for evaluation of suspected interstitial keratitis of the right eye. He noted progressive blurry vision but denied eye pain or antecedent trauma. Visual acuity on presentation was 20/50 OD and 20/20 OS. Examination of the right eye revealed a 5-mm inferonasal granular white opacity in the anterior corneal stroma without overlying epithelial defect. There were deep vessels visible in the anterior corneal stroma and Descemet membrane folds (Figure 1A). The remainder of the anterior segment was unremarkable. Anterior segment optical coherence tomography demonstrated a hyperreflective infiltrate in the area of the corneal opacity with associated corneal thickening (Figure 1B). Dilated fundus examination did not reveal any vitritis or retinal findings. Examination of the left eye was unremarkable. Medical history was remarkable for a 10–pack-year smoking history, stable thoracic aortic aneurysm, and hypertension. There was no history of contact lens wear. A review of systems was negative for a history of eye infections, travel outside of the US, or hearing changes. Limited workup was positive for herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1) and HSV2 immunoglobulin G (IgG) and negative for antinuclear antibody (ANA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), rapid plasma reagin (RPR), anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP), and interferon gamma release assay for tuberculosis. Given the positive HSV1 and HSV2 IgG and unremarkable preliminary autoimmune and infectious workup, the patient was given topical corticosteroids and oral valaciclovir for presumed herpetic interstitial keratitis.1,2His corneal opacity persisted despite this treatment.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform a corneal biopsy Corneal scraping and culture were not performed, given the intact corneal epithelium and lack of antecedent trauma or pain (option D). Given positive HSV antibodies and negative ANCA, ANA, and anti-CCP, there was low suspicion for an autoimmune etiology, and referral to rheumatology was deferred (option B). A diagnostic anterior chamber paracentesis was not performed, given the lack of anterior chamber inflammation (option A). A corneal biopsy was performed (option C), which showed a few keratinocytes as well as corneal edema and inflammation without deposits, granulomatous inflammation, or infectious organisms. The patient continued topical corticosteroids. Despite treatment, the patient re-presented with necrotizing scleritis and anterior segment neovascularization (Figure 2). Broad additional workups were performed in conjunction with rheumatology, including 2 additional corneal and scleral biopsies (without evidence of amyloid, infection, or neoplasia), erythrocyte sedimentation rate/C-reactive protein, fluorescein angiogram, carotid ultrasound (to evaluate for ocular ischemic syndrome), corneal scraping and culture, and hepatitis and HIV serologies, all of which were unrevealing, and the sclerokeratitis was attributed to an undifferentiated autoimmune process. Over the course of the next few months, the patient was stabilized receiving high-dose oral prednisone and rituximab. Eight months after initial presentation, visual acuity acutely worsened to light perception, and the patient developed a new afferent pupillary defect in the right eye with ptosis and limitations in upgaze and adduction. Magnetic resonance imaging at that time demonstrated asymmetric enhancement of the tendinous portion of the right inferior rectus. B-scan ultrasound was remarkable for choroidal effusions with overlying retinal detachment. He underwent biopsy of the sclera and orbit, which, along with genetic sequencing, revealed conjunctival adenosquamous carcinoma (Figure 2, inset). After diagnosis, the original sclerocorneal biopsy underwent additional sectioning, and a single distal section with a few atypical cells was detected. These stained positive for p40, which was also expressed in the tumor. This case represents a rare presentation of conjunctival adenosquamous carcinoma, masquerading as interstitial keratitis. Previously termed mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the ocular surface, conjunctival adenosquamous carcinoma, this tumor falls under the headingocular surface squamous cell neoplasia(OSSN).3This tumor is relatively rare, and to our knowledge, this was the first case of the tumor masquerading as interstitial keratitis.4There have been a few reports of OSSN masquerading as sclerokeratitis.5Interestingly, the majority of these cases, including the one case of OSSN presenting as interstitial keratitis, were definitively diagnosed as squamous cell carcinoma on the first biopsy.5-9 The patient’s immunosuppression was stopped, and the case was presented to tumor board. Orbital exenteration was recommended given the orbital extension of the malignancy, followed by intensity-modulated radiation therapy and adjuvant immunotherapy. The patient continues to have close follow-up for the first 2 years to monitor for recurrence, and recently, a metastasis to the abdominal muscles was discovered.10This case demonstrates the importance of revisiting a broad differential diagnosis if the disease is unresponsive to conventional therapy and the importance of communication with pathology, including requesting additional sectioning in atypical cases.

A corneal biopsy was performed (option C), which showed a few keratinocytes as well as corneal edema and inflammation without deposits, granulomatous inflammation, or infectious organisms. The patient continued topical corticosteroids. Despite treatment, the patient re-presented with necrotizing scleritis and anterior segment neovascularization (Figure 2). Broad additional workups were performed in conjunction with rheumatology, including 2 additional corneal and scleral biopsies (without evidence of amyloid, infection, or neoplasia), erythrocyte sedimentation rate/C-reactive protein, fluorescein angiogram, carotid ultrasound (to evaluate for ocular ischemic syndrome), corneal scraping and culture, and hepatitis and HIV serologies, all of which were unrevealing, and the sclerokeratitis was attributed to an undifferentiated autoimmune process. Over the course of the next few months, the patient was stabilized receiving high-dose oral prednisone and rituximab. Eight months after initial presentation, visual acuity acutely worsened to light perception, and the patient developed a new afferent pupillary defect in the right eye with ptosis and limitations in upgaze and adduction. Magnetic resonance imaging at that time demonstrated asymmetric enhancement of the tendinous portion of the right inferior rectus. B-scan ultrasound was remarkable for choroidal effusions with overlying retinal detachment. After diagnosis, the original sclerocorneal biopsy underwent additional sectioning, and a single distal section with a few atypical cells was detected. Given positive HSV antibodies and negative ANCA, ANA, and anti-CCP, there was low suspicion for an autoimmune etiology, and referral to rheumatology was deferred (option B). A diagnostic anterior chamber paracentesis was not performed, given the lack of anterior chamber inflammation (option A). A corneal biopsy was performed (option C), which showed a few keratinocytes as well as corneal edema and inflammation without deposits, granulomatous inflammation, or infectious organisms. The patient continued topical corticosteroids. Despite treatment, the patient re-presented with necrotizing scleritis and anterior segment neovascularization (Figure 2). Broad additional workups were performed in conjunction with rheumatology, including 2 additional corneal and scleral biopsies (without evidence of amyloid, infection, or neoplasia), erythrocyte sedimentation rate/C-reactive protein, fluorescein angiogram, carotid ultrasound (to evaluate for ocular ischemic syndrome), corneal scraping and culture, and hepatitis and HIV serologies, all of which were unrevealing, and the sclerokeratitis was attributed to an undifferentiated autoimmune process. Over the course of the next few months, the patient was stabilized receiving high-dose oral prednisone and rituximab. Eight months after initial presentation, visual acuity acutely worsened to light perception, and the patient developed a new afferent pupillary defect in the right eye with ptosis and limitations in upgaze and adduction. Magnetic resonance imaging at that time demonstrated asymmetric enhancement of the tendinous portion of the right inferior rectus. B-scan ultrasound was remarkable for choroidal effusions with overlying retinal detachment. He underwent biopsy of the sclera and orbit, which, along with genetic sequencing, revealed conjunctival adenosquamous carcinoma (Figure 2, inset). After diagnosis, the original sclerocorneal biopsy underwent additional sectioning, and a single distal section with a few atypical cells was detected. These stained positive for p40, which was also expressed in the tumor. This case represents a rare presentation of conjunctival adenosquamous carcinoma, masquerading as interstitial keratitis. Previously termed mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the ocular surface, conjunctival adenosquamous carcinoma, this tumor falls under the headingocular surface squamous cell neoplasia(OSSN).3This tumor is relatively rare, and to our knowledge, this was the first case of the tumor masquerading as interstitial keratitis.4There have been a few reports of OSSN masquerading as sclerokeratitis.5Interestingly, the majority of these cases, including the one case of OSSN presenting as interstitial keratitis, were definitively diagnosed as squamous cell carcinoma on the first biopsy.5-9 The patient’s immunosuppression was stopped, and the case was presented to tumor board. Orbital exenteration was recommended given the orbital extension of the malignancy, followed by intensity-modulated radiation therapy and adjuvant immunotherapy. The patient continues to have close follow-up for the first 2 years to monitor for recurrence, and recently, a metastasis to the abdominal muscles was discovered.10This case demonstrates the importance of revisiting a broad differential diagnosis if the disease is unresponsive to conventional therapy and the importance of communication with pathology, including requesting additional sectioning in atypical cases.

A corneal biopsy was performed (option C), which showed a few keratinocytes as well as corneal edema and inflammation without deposits, granulomatous inflammation, or infectious organisms. The patient continued topical corticosteroids. Despite treatment, the patient re-presented with necrotizing scleritis and anterior segment neovascularization (Figure 2). Broad additional workups were performed in conjunction with rheumatology, including 2 additional corneal and scleral biopsies (without evidence of amyloid, infection, or neoplasia), erythrocyte sedimentation rate/C-reactive protein, fluorescein angiogram, carotid ultrasound (to evaluate for ocular ischemic syndrome), corneal scraping and culture, and hepatitis and HIV serologies, all of which were unrevealing, and the sclerokeratitis was attributed to an undifferentiated autoimmune process. Over the course of the next few months, the patient was stabilized receiving high-dose oral prednisone and rituximab. Eight months after initial presentation, visual acuity acutely worsened to light perception, and the patient developed a new afferent pupillary defect in the right eye with ptosis and limitations in upgaze and adduction. Magnetic resonance imaging at that time demonstrated asymmetric enhancement of the tendinous portion of the right inferior rectus. B-scan ultrasound was remarkable for choroidal effusions with overlying retinal detachment. He underwent biopsy of the sclera and orbit, which, along with genetic sequencing, revealed conjunctival adenosquamous carcinoma (Figure 2, inset). After diagnosis, the original sclerocorneal biopsy underwent additional sectioning, and a single distal section with a few atypical cells was detected. These stained positive for p40, which was also expressed in the tumor. This case represents a rare presentation of conjunctival adenosquamous carcinoma, masquerading as interstitial keratitis. Orbital exenteration was recommended given the orbital extension of the malignancy, followed by intensity-modulated radiation therapy and adjuvant immunotherapy. The patient continues to have close follow-up for the first 2 years to monitor for recurrence, and recently, a metastasis to the abdominal muscles was discovered.10This case demonstrates the importance of revisiting a broad differential diagnosis if the disease is unresponsive to conventional therapy and the importance of communication with pathology, including requesting additional sectioning in atypical cases.
